entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Servius Cornelius Dolabella Petronianus was a Roman senator in the latter part of the first century AD, holding the significant position of colleague to the emperor Domitian. As one of the eponymous consuls of AD 86, he played a crucial role in the governance of Rome during a period of relative stability and prosperity.

Petronianus's influence extended beyond his official capacity, as he was also a prominent figure in the intellectual and cultural circles of the Roman elite. His connections with other notable figures of the time, including the statesman and philosopher Publius Aelius Seianus, demonstrate the importance of his position within the imperial administration.

Despite the relative calm of the late first century AD, Petronianus's legacy would eventually contribute to the turbulent events of the late second century, as the Roman Empire began to face internal strife and external pressures. His tenure as consul of AD 86 marked the beginning of a period of increasing instability, which would ultimately lead to the rise of the Year of the Four Emperors and the eventual collapse of the Roman Empire.

In the centuries that followed, Petronianus's name would become synonymous with the tumultuous period of Roman history that he helped shape. As a testament to his enduring impact, the Roman historian Tacitus would later write of Petronianus's role in the reign of Domitian, highlighting the senator's critical role in the events that would ultimately lead to the downfall of the emperor.
